title: Juno: Into the Heart of Jupiter
intro: A solar-powered spacecraft crossed 1.7 billion miles of space to reach Jupiter. What it found beneath the giant planet's clouds changed our view of the solar system's largest world.

chapters.heading: The journey begins
main: Juno launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, aboard an Atlas V rocket, beginning a nearly five-year journey to Jupiter.
Unlike earlier spacecraft sent toward the giant planet, Juno was designed to investigate what lies beneath Jupiter's spectacular cloud tops.
chapters.frame: A rocket rises from Cape Canaveral, carrying Juno toward the outer solar system.
chapters.extra:
The mission

Juno was built to study Jupiter's atmosphere, gravity field, magnetic field, auroras and interior. Understanding Jupiter can reveal clues about how the solar system formed.

By the numbers

  • Launch: August 5, 2011
  • Destination: Jupiter
  • Journey to Jupiter: about 1.7 billion miles (2.8 billion kilometers)

chapters.heading: A boost from Earth
main: Juno returned toward Earth instead of heading directly for Jupiter. On October 9, 2013, it flew past our planet and used Earth's gravity to gain speed.
The maneuver gave Juno the extra push needed to continue its journey into the outer solar system.
chapters.frame: Juno sweeps past Earth, with the planet filling the spacecraft's view.
chapters.extra:
Gravity assist

Juno's flight path was designed to use Earth's gravity as a natural boost. The spacecraft had traveled about 994 million miles (1.6 billion kilometers) by the time of the Earth flyby.

A close pass

At its closest point, Juno passed about 500 kilometers above Earth's surface.

chapters.heading: Into Jupiter's orbit
main: After almost five years in space, Juno finally reached Jupiter. The spacecraft had to slow itself down with a precisely timed engine burn.
For about 35 minutes, Juno's main engine fired. When the burn ended, the spacecraft had been captured by Jupiter's gravity.
chapters.frame: Juno approaches Jupiter from above its north pole as the enormous planet fills the screen.
chapters.extra:
A critical moment

Juno was too far from Earth for controllers to make last-second corrections. Radio signals took about 48 minutes to travel one way between Jupiter and Earth at the time of orbit insertion.

The new orbit

Juno entered a highly elliptical polar orbit that carried it from close above Jupiter's clouds to the distant reaches of the planet's magnetic environment.

chapters.heading: A planet without a surface
main: Jupiter has no solid surface for Juno to land on. Instead, the spacecraft repeatedly dived close to the cloud tops, passing through an environment filled with intense radiation.
Its instruments measured Jupiter's gravity and magnetic fields while observing the atmosphere from a perspective no previous orbiter had achieved.
chapters.frame: Juno dives toward Jupiter's cloud tops, then pulls away into the darkness of space.
chapters.extra:
Built for radiation

Juno's most sensitive electronics are protected inside a titanium radiation vault. The spacecraft was designed specifically to survive the extreme environment around Jupiter.

What Juno was looking for

  • The structure of Jupiter's interior
  • Water and ammonia deep in the atmosphere
  • The origin of Jupiter's magnetic field
  • The mechanisms behind Jupiter's powerful auroras

chapters.heading: The storms go deep
main: Juno revealed that Jupiter's familiar belts and zones are not just a thin layer of clouds. Measurements showed that the powerful jet streams extend roughly 3,000 kilometers beneath the cloud tops.
The spacecraft was beginning to show that Jupiter's atmosphere is a much deeper and more complex system than scientists once thought.
chapters.frame: Colorful bands of Jupiter rotate beneath Juno as invisible layers of atmosphere are revealed.
chapters.extra:
Gravity as a probe

Juno measures tiny variations in Jupiter's gravity field as it passes over different parts of the planet. Those measurements allow scientists to investigate structures hidden beneath the clouds.

A deeper Jupiter

The atmospheric belts and zones were found to penetrate far deeper into the planet than many earlier models suggested.

chapters.heading: A giant moon appears
main: Juno's mission expanded beyond Jupiter itself. On June 7, 2021, the spacecraft flew close to Ganymede, Jupiter's largest moon.
The encounter was the closest spacecraft visit to Ganymede in more than two decades and gave scientists a remarkably detailed new view of the icy world.
chapters.frame: Ganymede grows from a distant point into a huge, cratered moon beneath Juno.
chapters.extra:
Changing the mission

Ganymede's gravity altered Juno's orbit, shortening the time between close passes around Jupiter.

A new phase

The extended mission allowed Juno to investigate several of Jupiter's major moons, adding new targets to a mission originally focused primarily on the giant planet.

chapters.heading: Europa comes closer
main: Juno continued its extended mission with a close encounter with Europa, one of Jupiter's most intriguing moons.
The flyby provided new observations of Europa's icy surface and helped reshape Juno's orbit for later encounters with other moons.
chapters.frame: Europa's bright icy surface passes beneath the spacecraft, scarred by long fractures.
chapters.extra:
Why Europa matters

Europa is an icy world of major interest to planetary scientists. Juno's observations added to the growing picture of Jupiter's complex moon system.

Orbit changes

The encounter reduced Juno's orbital period again, setting up later close encounters with Io.

chapters.heading: The volcanic world
main: Juno turned its attention toward Io, the most volcanically active world known in the solar system. Close encounters brought the spacecraft near the moon's surface and its enormous volcanic activity.
The observations added another chapter to Juno's exploration of Jupiter's extraordinary family of moons.
chapters.frame: A glowing volcanic plume rises from Io's surface while Jupiter hangs enormous in the background.
chapters.extra:
Io

Juno made close encounters with Io in December 2023 and February 2024. The spacecraft observed volcanic features and the interaction between Io and Jupiter's powerful magnetic environment.

A changing orbit

After the moon encounters, Juno moved into its final extended-mission orbital pattern around Jupiter.

chapters.heading: The final chapter
main: After years of revealing Jupiter's hidden structure, Juno's extended mission reached its planned end in September 2025.
Its journey transformed Jupiter from a distant striped world into a dynamic planet with deep atmospheric currents, a powerful magnetic environment and a remarkable family of active moons.
chapters.frame: Juno disappears into the darkness as Jupiter fills the final frame.
chapters.extra:
The legacy

Juno's measurements continue to help scientists understand Jupiter's origin and evolution, and what those clues can tell us about the formation of giant planets and the solar system.

The final fate

Juno was designed to ultimately enter Jupiter's atmosphere and burn up, helping protect Jupiter's potentially habitable moons from accidental contamination by material from Earth.
